result:
In the town where lost time collected, the clocks had no hands.

People arrived carrying the usual regrets: years spent in the wrong profession, afternoons surrendered to worry, the last ten minutes of a conversation they had ended too soon. They came because they’d heard you could get some of it back.

This was not quite true.

At the station, a woman in a green coat sorted time into wooden drawers.

“Was it wasted,” she asked each visitor, “or did you simply not enjoy it?”

Most people needed to sit down after that.

One man brought seventeen years of waiting for his life to begin. The woman examined them under a lamp.

“There are some perfectly good Tuesdays in here,” she said.

“I didn’t notice.”

“No. That happens.”

She returned one to him.

He found himself in his old kitchen, younger but not young, with rain tapping the window. There was a pear on the counter. Upstairs, someone he loved was moving furniture for no clear reason.

He remembered this day. Nothing had happened.

This time, he ate the pear. It was ripe enough that he had to lean over the sink. Then he went upstairs to see whether he could help.

Others received smaller things: a bus ride, a bath, twenty minutes before the guests arrived.

A girl asked for a summer back.

The woman opened several drawers, then closed them.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “We don’t have whole summers.”

“What do you have?”

“A morning. Your father is teaching you to whistle.”

“Will I remember what happens afterward?”

“Yes.”

The girl stood a long time beside the counter. Then she held out her hand.
